Theme able spreadsheet with bugs (nice to read NULL on stuff). Ideologies, etc. are number buffs/debuffs. While it has a great number of variables and numbers to change and numbers affecting other numbers it's really just that and very deterministic which means it cannot live up to simulating real socio-economy, butterfly effects. This makes it feel like highly naive take on economics, politics and sociology. Another perspective where this is highly visible is the tech tree. Three categories where the connections feel random and like just a very forced way of balanced progression. To give more examples, there is a "standard of living" that just instantly increases/decreases for everyone and things that are a "minimum requirement" that other actions lower/increase instantly, like editing a spreadsheet. Everything is also an on/off switch. Buff/debuff support for a group, You click on "Collectivize Agriculture" and the hivemind of your population even in the most remote area magically instantly applies it 100%, as if the research were "invent a magical button". And all of them. No matter how much they like your government, no matter their ideology, or how close they are to starting a revolution. That said though, if you really are into deterministic spreadsheet style games, number optimization and so on this game might still be for you. Those things are fine, but maybe don't call it a simulation of politics/history and don't pretend that you are simulating all of your population or something. Politics, history, etc. are more complex. Even adding a bit more RNG would probably do a better job. Right now it seems to just randomly be thrown into law making which feels quite an odd place and sometimes very odd when you have a quite authoritarian government. Doesn't seem to be the place where a decision should drag on for months based on dice rolls.

More variety would be nice, but not at all the issue I have with Shadows of Doubt. The game just doesn't perform well at all. I've played it on a handful of PCs and even after upgrading to an RTX card to deal with the forced ray tracing here it's always the same. If your game struggles to meet a stable 30 fps on a modern gaming rig while running at 640x480 resolution on the lowest settings available, something is fundamentally wrong with it. Indoors the game does better, but unless you're like me and are occasionally willing to cap the frame rate to 24 @ 800x600 to make it an "analog cinematic experience", it's gonna be a very rough ride. (I'd have stuck with 640x480, but none of the UI scales so everything below 800x600 is totally illegible.)

Every part of Qud's design that involves creativity is brilliant. Every part of it that involves judgement, or seeing the big picture, is totally incompetent. It's also a game that seems to resent its players and that is actively hostile to their understanding of the game world. First, the game generates visual scenes with are utterly incomprehensible, due its the haphazard, thoughtless map generation algorithms. I have never played a game where it felt worse to try to stumble through level maps, because they are absolutely crammed full of tiles that block movement, or sight, or both. The number of these blocking tiles would literally need to be decreased by a factor of two or three to be acceptable. The map generation process doesn't verify the inside of structures it generates connect to the outside. It doesn't even make sure the player isn't trapped in one of these inaccessible spaces when they enter a level. Awful, low contrast color choices make it hard to tell apart tiles from actors or tiles from other tiles. And that's before the screen gets smeared with blood and gunk and slime. Over the course of battle, characters leak an absurd amount of fluid. And it just builds up, and builds up. Your character slips on it and steps in it. Sometimes these fluids are harmful, and sometimes the does warn you before you step on a harmful tile...And sometimes it doesn't. Autoexplore can kill you. The level of message spam the game throws at you is bizarre. The message buffer narrates every time you walk under a tree...Even if the tree does nothing. The message buffer is the entire length of the screen on the right side, and yet it still barely keeps up with all the meaningless nonsense messages the game drowns you in. Oh, if there is some sort of environmental fluid on equipment you use or encounter, get ready for an even longer description to be crammed into the buffer each time you attack with it. The game is possessed of cascading effects that are ignorant of each other, and difficulty is completely uneven. At certain break points in stats, damage is multiplied many times over, meaning that you can go from enemies being fairly harmless at some stat levels to killing you in a few shots at slightly higher levels. Experience rewards make no sense based on how difficult enemies are to kill. Some types of end game enemies are assigned random abilities, and this means an enemy with exactly the same appearance can be either a deadly threat or trivial. Finally, it's a game with so many interface screws on top of it's already obfuscated visual style. You can go colorblind. The screen gets scrambled when you are confused. The names of your items are scrambled when you are confused. For all these reasons, I've never played a game where I said more often "I don't know what just happened." Understand this: Qud is a meme game. You can post interesting stories about it online, like the time you got "crungled by a dreamcrungle". But actually playing it is like wading through sewage.

The game is pretty fun when you are just starting out and discovering everything. It's also pretty unique and tries something that is the game industry is really lacking right now. I'd recommend it if the devs were trying to improve it, but that does not seem to be the case, so I'll judge it as a finished product. For something that calls itself a "immersive detective simulator", this game isn't immersive at all. The worst offender is probably the complete lack of consequences for player actions. You can break into a guy's house, knock out his wife in front of him, open his safe, steal all his stuff, go out the front door and run away for like 10 to 20 seconds, then come back, knock on his door, ask him to come in and he's like "Of course, make yourself at home :)". All your crimes are pardoned and you don't even have to return the $20k diamonds you stolen right in front of him and 2 cameras. Because of this, if you want money to mean anything, you pretty much need to make it a house rule not to steal anything. The NPCs really feel like lifeless robots. They will never remember you or anything you done, your interaction with them is very limited and they're usually pretty unhelpful, which is really sad since interrogation is a big part of investigation. You can ask an NPC about the victim and they'll respond like "Oh yeah, I saw them near X" as if they were still alive and walking around. The partner of a victim is just as likely to let you inside their house to investigate (or be helpful in any kind of way) as the murderer. If someone is murdered inside their house and they have a partner, the partner will stand outside the house knocking on the door trying to get in as if nothing happened. In fact, the entire NPCs routine is very weird and buggy. Speaking of which, there are also tons of bugs, but I didn't find anything game-breaking while I was playing. The procedural generation is OK, sometimes it generates broken stuff but there is a good variety of NPCs, buildings, rooms, notes, emails, even cases. It's pretty impressive. However, due to the nature of it, things are bound to start repeating. I had 2 murder cases back to back that were basically the same case with different NPCs. The side jobs can generate some really insane cases like "find this person, they have blue eyes, blond hair and their shoe size is 14. Good luck :)". Overall, I'd say the game is decent, though I expected more. You can definitely play it for a while as long as you don't expect much of it. The biggest issue to me is that it's very easy to see the "cracks in the simulation", so it's very difficult to get immersed, which seems to be what this game tried to do.

Shadows of Doubt has the perfect basis for a really solid detective game If you actually would play a detective instead of a robber or a bully Everything about this game has potential but said potential never gets fully realized, and its disheartening honestly. The Enforcers are basically useless and are just there to come if someone gets murdered or kidnapped to tape the area and guard the door. They could be more interesting if I could bribe them to make my own crimes go away. If they would actually investigate my own crimes I do, which they should do. There could also be a huge cover-up or other types of corruption case with the enforcers. Bribe them to get into places. Ya could get a job to frame somebody and call the enforcers on them. How civilians work need to be overhauled because just throwing an object onto the street like a bottle of alcohol will make them hostile and even attack you. They also react to your crimes and attack you. There needs to be more of a bystander effect where they either call enforcers or just ignore it. Civilians also need more random events onto the streets, the default one is just being robbed by one. But what about stopping others from being robbed, attacked etc? Maybe you catch 2 people arguing which can turn out to be a case? It has endless possibilities. How you also finish jobs is extremely repetitive and its either extremely easy or borderline impossible. *Has Long Hair* *Suffers from Alcoholism* Great, how the hell should I figure out my target with that? Especially with the limited options I have to ask people. All your info you get from a government database anyway. You can just go into cityhall, go onto a enforcer computer which you are just allowed to access. Buy the extremely cheap codebreaker for 75 bucks and you're good to go. And its in an area where you aren't marked as a trespasser. More options would be nice. Maybe search options instead of names at certain locations. As an example of what could be different: Your target had an alcoholism problem and was recently released from rehab. You break into said center and try to find any person who had been recently released, had an alcoholism problem and also other descriptive features. Or maybe bribe someone to get you said info. Huge potential to more facilities where you can get info from. Right now its just workspaces, patient records and government database, but they all work the same way by typing in names. Government Database should only work with names, workspaces too. Patient records should work with names, symptoms and other afflictions. The type of jobs could be expanded. Yes the game has a workshop, but should fans take up the slack and make THE detective game? Maybe. Or they should work on a sequel that fixes all these problems. IT IS still a very fun game and its still very unique

When I boot up a fantasy story or a game on that genre, I expect characters with different classes (swordsman, thief, mage...) to represent different backgrounds, upbringings and/or moral choices. A mage doesn't necessarily have to be a smart person, but, he has to have come from a mentor (or some tough self-learning) that leaned him towards certain life goals involving knowledge, regardless to whether he feels connected to these goals or not. When I see a werewolf character, I expect him to struggle with issues like self control, self worth... or at least address them in some way due to their inevitable messy nature. Wildermyth, however, doesn't tackle issues like that in any way. Your characters already start as warrior, archer and mage (the only 3 classes of the game) without being tied to anything, and they can transform themselves into wolves, skeletons and elemental forms without any changes in their goals or how society views them whatsoever. It's a shame, because I really like the premise of this game design, but in the end, the lack of worldbuilding being tied to what each class (and transformatiom) can do turned my experience into a big pile of blankness. You do get choice/generated romances, friendships and rivalries, but they also feel empty due to not being tied into morals, upbringings or goals. If this system was tied to meaningful worldbuilding, I feel like my experience would have been 1000x better.

Like many of the other reviews stated, the game is broken. I spent a good 30 minutes to an hour reading the negative reviews and crying laughing at how ridiculous the bugs are. So I'll contribute my experience too for others' entertainment. To set the scene, you start a sandbox game loading a pre-made map you've spent 3-5 minutes waiting for to load. Finally finished roleplaying the down-on-his-luck detective waiting aimlessly for something to happen, you decide to pick up a side job from the pinboard of the telephone booth of the random diner you found yourself in. You eagerly pick up the phone to call the associated number for more details only to be told to pick up a phone that's due to ring 2 minutes from then in a café on the other side of the map you aren't yet familiar with. You hang up as soon as you can to make sure you don't miss the call only to be met with "side quest failed" before you've even stepped your big toe out the door. Not to worry, after countless hours waiting in real time, you finally get news of a murder to be investigated. You make your way to city hall to pick up the case report and head to the scene of the crime. The place is still riddled with enforcers so you need to be sneaky. You peak your head round the corner and instantly alert everyone in the immediate vicinity including the security system turrets, that kill you within seconds. That's okay, we all make mistakes, thank god there's minimal penalty for your shortcomings. Or so you thought. You wake up standing next to the hospital bed you're supposed to be lying in, with the security system alarm blasting. You're unable to select any of the options on your screen asking you to pay the medical bills or choose to flee resulting in being shot infinitely in the back by turrets while all actions are rendered unavailable because the game thinks you're simultaneously lying in bed AND actively attempting to flee, meaning you can't die! The results are always the same, delete the save and start completely fresh... again. All these exciting game breaking bugs aside, I don't want to miss out the sprinkles of emersion breaking features the game also offers. For example, the lightspeed visual textures that appear when making your way through the vent system. Or, the fact that NPCs will gladly let you wander their homes upon first meeting but refuse to give you their name or even tell you how they're doing. On top of that, the "choice" to do things by the law or illegally is non-existent due to the completely uncooperative NPCs at every turn who make you either beat them up, break into their home or steal belongings just to have even a shred of information to work with. It's just "home invasion simulator" dressed up as a dystopian detective game. When I played this game in early access I was so excited by this unique concept and promising execution. Now the game is literally unplayable and it doesn't matter what I do, I will inevitably end up dying and having to completely trash the save. I have no hopes that the developers will improve these issues, therefore I do not recommend purchasing the game.

I cannot say if it's a good game or not in the long run. What I *can* say is that it is in no way beginner-friendly. It has a tutorial, but it is not very helpful. The main issue is the UI, because while I can respect the fact that it's a very complicated game, the presentation of information is overwhelming. Let's look at an example, my attempt at the *first* tutorial (which I got 6 hours into before giving up): So, I get a warning that my chosen nation's (relative) status is weakening. To maintain or increase my standing, I need Prestige. This is a "basket" resource comprised of other factors, such as GDP, military might, and so on. I'm already building my industries, so I will try to focus more on that. I have recently invented railroads, which needs coal to run, so I decide to build a coal mine while also developing my first railroads. Only one of my provinces presents coal mines as an option, along with a tooltip telling me that a mine will not produce anything. No idea why. I still build it, because while other nations might sell some coal, I don't have anything I could trade for it. After some time, the mine finishes building, and sure enough, produces nothing because nobody goes to work there. There's plenty of job-seekers, so no idea why. Then my railroad finishes building. Oh no, now I need Engines. Engines are produced from Steel, which also needs coal. Probably close to half of my 6 hours of playtime I've spent Paused while looking into menus, trying to find the information that helps me understand something. But honestly, when I started looking at Citizenship policies and I'm presented with probably around 30 effects that policy would have on my society, and I have no idea what any of that means, I'm giving up. I don't mind that abundance of information existing, but a summary (ie. "This policy grants group X more rights and makes them politically stronger and stable, while weakening and angering group Y.") would be immensely more helpful. I really wish I could get into it, but this is a consistent problem with Paradox games. The tutorial would be much more helpful if it handed down a small nation and guiding you through its development, than tossing you into the gears of an already running complex machine. As it stands learning curve uppercuts you right on the doormat that says "Welcome", instead of padding it out in the longer haul.

When considering purchasing this "game" one must sit and ponder just how much time they are willing to waste to play this game as intended by the developers. On average without any mods construction which is a key component of the "gameplay" and essential for economic growth progresses at a absolute snails pace with your whole nation's worth of budget and construction sectors only able to build maybe 14 buildings in about 24 in game weeks for each building. However you might be thinking "Hay it can't be that bad it's only one aspect of the game and since this is a paradox game surly the war/military can't be that bad" but you'd be mistaken. As some might know, normally in paradox games such as Victoria 2, EU4, Imperator Rome, or Hearts of Iron you manually command your armies about the map which gives the player something to do while waiting for things such as buildings to be completed or colonies to finish and is generally the most entertaining part of these games. But this time in Vitoria 3 paradox decided to completely gut the war system and instead replaced player controlled armies and navies with brain dead "generals" which take their 369 unit army consisting of artillery, tanks, and trench infantry and then engage a army of 15 units with 5 units entirely consisting of artillery and get curb stomped. As previously mentioned this game is best used as a screen saver as the only time I really "play" this game is when I'm doing something else while this game runs in the background. I really wanted to like this game, as I adore cozy games, being a cozy little guy myself. The thing is, the world feels kind of empty and one dimensional, the combat is boring, and progression isn't satisfying. There's no motivation to explore, as chests and secrets are more or less useless, and much of the environment feels stamped and homogeneous. Once you get past the light saturation, it could be a very pretty game with just a touch more effort. I'm all for the cartoon art style, but something about this doesn't quite hit right. Maybe it goes back to the lighting engine. Very flat shadows, nothing pretty to look at volumetrically or even on backdrops such as stars or sunsets. The combat is so bland and repetitive that I actually found myself dreading it and going out of my way to avoid it. There's no gimmicks, let alone actual mechanics. It's just ping pong with damage numbers. And as for item progression, you start out with a small backpack that forces you to shuttle items like mad, and end with a bunch of chests to dump items from a backpack that never quite gets large enough. So you end where you started. Shuttling items like mad. Except now you have to sort everything. And weapons change a little bit. Also at some point five gidgets made one gadget but now a hundred widgets make one wadget. They forced a little Stardew Valley in there somehow with the whole relationship thing. But without the rich storytelling it was just sort of there. I wasn't drawn into that at all. It's a cute game, and I adore the concept. I would definitely buy it on sale, but don't expect a lot from it. Maybe a few days at best, but don't expect replayability or to stay entertained for very long.

The near thousand hours Steam says I've put in feel kind of misleading - but even if you only count the times I've actually played an entire character through, without mod troubleshooting or false starts, it's still a lot of hours. And they've been fun hours! I really really want to like this game, and I really really want to keep playing it. So why the "not recommend"? I just keep thinking about the one experience that makes me not want to go back to this game, despite all that. I was playing the Wallada bint Al-Mustakfi bookmark start, which starts you as a Muslim poet adventurer in Spain. Really fascinating woman in history, and I wanted to try out the adventurer mechanics. Eventually, I got to the point where I could host a Camp Revelry and invite the leader of the Almoravids himself, as well as his family. All well and good... until a random member of my camp murdered his son and heir. Immediately really interesting, right? It's a story that writes itself, an event that could shape the history of the rest of the game - on TV this would be an incredible cliffhanger. And the game presents me with the perfect options for it. Do I keep the murder a secret? That could mean protecting myself and my camp from the potential ramifications of having someone in my own camp kill the prince of the Almoravids. Or do I reveal the killer? That's risky, but could show I wasn't responsible for his actions in the hopes that the king will be less wrathful. Thinking carefully, I chose to reveal the murderer, and... Nothing happens. Nothing happens at all. The murderer was put in my own prison instead, and I can't even execute him despite the severity of his crime, for some reason. The leader of the Almoravids has no reaction to his son being killed during this event. My relationship with him doesn't change. The entire camp revelry activity moves on as if this event, something that should cause total upheaval in my camp and in the Almoravid dynasty, was just another Tuesday. And that's just... boring? What's even the point of having a random murder event if there's no consequences? Why can a random murder target in a random activity target emperors and heirs if their families don't care? What is the point of the event system at all if it can't actually be used to tell meaningful stories? And that's the entire problem with this game, the event system. The events are everywhere in this game, to the point there are multiple paid DLCs that consist entirely of events or are glorified events, and none of it matters. The majority of events involve completely random characters that are generated on-the-fly for the event, and are then deleted, so it's impossible for there to be actual narrative consequences. Many other events are simplistic "raise your relationship with a character, lower it with another" or "have two characters increase or decrease their relationship with another," but this is narratively toothless because these relationship scores barely matter. As the player, keeping them raised is completely trivial, and with NPC-to-NPC relationships, it's effectively invisible. Even with NPCs that should be important, only events in the same event chain have any continuity, so there's no drama. Most decisions you make in events involving, say, your vassals, only affect their relationship points with you and/or with each other... and that's it. A common type of event is two vassals asking you to choose which of them you favor, but nobody "remembers" your choices here. It'll raise your relationship points with the one you favor, but he won't bring it up later in an unrelated event to show his loyalty to you. It'll cause the relationship values between the two vassals to decrease if you fail a diplomacy check, but this won't ever cause a spiral where your slighted vassals ally with each other and take sides, because none of your other vassals or their friends or family care. Is expecting a detailed simulation of interpersonal character dynamics unreasonable? Maybe. But there are so many events, some of which you pay money for, and so many of them are repetitive and uninteresting and don't make any meaningful difference in the narrative of the game. This is a game that wants to be about roleplaying and characters just as much as, if not more than, strategy, where the roleplaying isn't interesting and the characters feel lifeless. It feels like the Sims but you have to read a bad book every 30 seconds. And, yeah, I'd probably be able to forgive this more if the writing was up to par. It's not. It's legitimately embarrassing. The writing feels downright juvenile, between the constant toilet humor and the writing about sex that would feel subpar even for dime-store bodice rippers, but all of the writing is bad. I'm a writer and it's hard to describe it other than that it feels like it's written for high schoolers, if that. The prose and dialogue are stiff and clunky, especially because the events are designed to slot in with every possible character on the map, regardless of culture, personality, or religion. This results in prose and dialogue that feel like mad libs - just look how many times the writing is very clearly written for Christian characters first, and then has to awkwardly rename "angels" and "devils" or "the Bible" to make it work for every other religion in the game. This is all made to feel even more embarrassing and juvenile because of the animations. For all the pride Paradox put into the 3D character models, the animations are simultaneously overanimated and stiff and awkward. You'll get sick of seeing the animation for a character gesturing angrily for ten seconds really fast, and characters doing the same "raise goblet and drink" animation at the exact same time just looks stupid. Ultimately, this just feels like how I really wanted to enjoy Skyrim, but couldn't, no matter how much I tried to mod it into something I'd enjoy more. I just don't think this part of the game is salvageable. Even with a huge amount of rewrites, even reanimating all of the awkward animations, you'd need to seriously overhaul how the events function from the ground up. The alternative is to wait for seasons and seasons of DLC to make the moment-to-moment gameplay more interesting, without relying on the events at all, and the game's heading in the right direction for that... but it's just not there yet. And, in its current form, I don't think it's worth it.

the game was free for a while when they announced the sequel thats when i grabbed it and gave it a try here are my thoughts The game isn't really about the graveyard but more about holding a single button to progress through the day cycle to get to the next day so you can walk 10 miles to talk to an npc to finish a quest and progress the story. By the time i finished the game i buried roughly 20 corpses, burned 40 and made 12 zombies. Negatives: - The story has loads of spelling mistakes later on - Early dungeon enemys have no cooldown on their attacks and your range is very limited making later enemys easy in comparison - The fishing mini game likes bugging out (not starting but playing the sound of fishing anyways until you either hit the timing again or fail) - The base game itself feels more like a demo (i played without any dlc and it was very noticeable) - Alchemy is either using the wiki or bashing your head against the wall - I unlocked the tutorial roughly 30 hours in after finding out that you can throw corpses into the river from the wiki, wouldve been nice for that to be a little more obvious - Locking the ability to see body part traits (making the corpse and graveyard refinement a guessing game) to the last quest in the game is a choice for sure - There is no way to increase your personal inventory size - Roughly 80 of the achievements are locked behind dlc (and im guessing an equal amount of content) - The ending scene basically just tells you to buy the dlc. Positives: - the music is really good - selling burgers and beer while a witch is being burned goes kinda hard 20 bucks would probably be fair if all the dlcs were included but without them its basically just a demo tips in case you wanna play anyways: 1.At the start of the game exhume the body with the most red skulls and throw it into the river on the left side of the graveyard to get an actually usefull tutorial that i completely missed. 2.Buy 1 teleporter stone from the tavern asap (it has a global cooldown and infinite uses, it will safe a lot of time). 3.Always take blood, fat and bones from bodys 4.Porter zombies do not benefit from white skulls so dont waste your good organs on them. 5.The only consequence to death is being teleported to your bed. No time advancement, no inventory loss. 6.Wine is probably the best and easiest to get resource for healing and stamina regen in the dungeon seeds can be aquired from >the merchant<. 7.Keep gold and silver nuggets for alchemy you'll need it for embalming.
